tagline.text: A canyon of split rock where revolutionaries hid and founded a republic

children.text: A national park set in a canyon at the foot of the Sierra Madre in San Miguel, Bulacan, where Aguinaldo's revolutionary forces based themselves in caves in 1897 and founded the Republic of Biak-na-Bato. With over a hundred caves, a clear river, a suspension bridge, and forest trails, it's a place to explore history and nature together.
Biak-na-Bato National Park is a protected area in San Miguel, Bulacan, about
80km

northeast of Manila. Most of the park lies within San Miguel's Biak-na-Bato village, extending into neighboring San Ildefonso and Doña Remedios Trinidad, for a total area of about 2,117 hectares. "Biak-na-Bato" is Tagalog for "split rock," named for the canyon landscape carved from Sierra Madre limestone by the Balaong River.

This is an important site in Philippine revolutionary history. Pursued by Spanish forces, Emilio Aguinaldo led his elite troops into this rugged canyon and set up headquarters in a cave, adopting a constitution modeled on Cuba's and proclaiming the Republic of Biak-na-Bato on
November 1, 1897
. The republic lasted just over a month, ending when Aguinaldo and his party went into exile in Hong Kong under the Pact of Biak-na-Bato, signed with the Spanish governor-general on
December 14, 1897
. To honor this history, President Manuel Quezon designated the site a national park in

The park holds over a hundred caves large and small. The best known are Aguinaldo Cave, the revolutionaries' headquarters, and Bahay Paniki (Bat Cave), home to colonies of bats; along the forest trails you'll also find a river and small waterfalls running between limestone cliffs, a suspension bridge crossing the river, and traces of old sentry posts and stone forts. Trinidad Tecson, a woman who carried food and medicine to the revolutionaries and tended the wounded, also came from this area and is known as "the Mother of Biak-na-Bato."

Facilities are modest for the size of the park, and the caves are dark with plenty of slippery spots, giving the visit a light sense of real exploration. It suits families and groups of friends near Manila who want to combine history, forest trekking, and swimming in one trip, and beginner hikers looking to pair it with a climb up neighboring Mount Manalmon.

The cave the revolutionary leadership used as headquarters in 1897, still showing several room-like chambers and a high ceiling. Walking through the spot where Aguinaldo held meetings and stayed, with a guide's commentary, brings the history from the textbooks vividly to life.

A cave where thousands of bats hang from the ceiling, with stalactites reaching down from above. The floor is muddy and the smell strong, so bring a headlamp and shoes you don't mind ruining. Don't flash a camera at the bats.

blocks.title: The Balaong River and small waterfalls

children.text: Clear river water flows between white limestone rocks, with small weirs and waterfalls scattered along the way. In the dry season, the shallow pools are good for dipping your feet and resting. Tilandong Falls, also inside the park, can be visited with a guide.
A trail through bamboo and tropical forest crosses a suspension bridge, linking the caves and viewpoints on a route you can cover in about
2–3 hours
. Morning, when the forest is full of birdsong, is the best time to walk.

blocks.title: Traces of revolutionary sentry posts and stone forts

children.text: Scattered around the park are the sites of sentry posts that once watched for approaching Spanish troops, traces of stone defensive works, and rocks carved with old inscriptions. Ask your guide where to find them.
Mount Manalmon (about
high) on the park's north side is a short climb mixing river crossings and rock scrambling; the summit, reachable in around
1 hour
, offers a view over the Sierra Madre range. Visit Madlum Cave and its river at the trailhead too.
San Miguel is known for milk sweets like pastillas and yema made from carabao milk. Even the old place name "Mayumo" means "sweet." Stop at a sweets shop along Maharlika Highway on your way back.

A private or chartered vehicle makes it easier to combine both in one day, and since afternoon showers are frequent in the wet season, finish the river crossing for the hike early in the morning, as it can be dangerous.
From Cubao in Manila, take a bus to San Miguel (Baliwag Transit, Five Star, and others) or a bus toward Gapan or Cabanatuan, and get off at the Camias (tricycle stand) in San Miguel. It takes about
2–3 hours
and costs about
You can also take a bus from Manila to Tabang near the NLEX Santa Rita exit, then transfer to a jeepney running between Tabang and Gapan, getting off in San Miguel.
From downtown San Miguel to the park entrance is about
10km
east, roughly
20–30 minutes
by tricycle. A one-way charter costs about
, and since it's hard to catch a ride back near the park, negotiate a round trip with waiting time included.
Exit NLEX at Santa Rita and follow Maharlika Highway through Plaridel and San Ildefonso, then turn onto the Biak-na-Bato road at San Miguel. It takes about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
from Manila, and there's parking at the park entrance.
To avoid traffic in Baliwag town, it's faster to leave the NLEX at the Balagtas exit, take the Plaridel Bypass (Route 247, about
, free), meet the Maharlika Highway at Maasim in San Rafael, and then head north to San Miguel.

Inside the park, you can only get around on foot. The paths linking the main caves and the river mix steps, dirt trail, rocks, and the suspension bridge, so sneakers or trekking sandals are needed. There's no lighting inside the caves, so bring a headlamp.
Biak-na-Bato, inland in central Luzon, has a clearly defined dry and wet season. In the dry season,
November–April
, the river runs clear and shallow, good for exploring the caves and riverside, and
December–February
has the coolest morning air, best suited to trekking.
March–May
sees midday temperatures climb to
, so plan to move in the morning.
From
late May
, when the wet season begins, through
October

, afternoon thunderstorms are frequent, and rain upstream can cause flash floods that raise the river in an instant. In fact, in 2004 and 2014, people swimming in the nearby Madlum River were swept away by sudden currents. The park sometimes closes when a typhoon signal is raised, so check PAGASA forecasts and park notices before visiting. During Holy Week, roads get crowded with crowds visiting the nearby pilgrimage site Banal na Bundok.

As a day trip from Manila, Biak-na-Bato has no lodging inside the park itself. If you'd rather take your time, use a small hotel or guesthouse (about

per night) in downtown San Miguel or in neighboring San Ildefonso or Gapan, Nueva Ecija. Some places near the Mount Manalmon trailhead accept campers, but management and rules change often, so inquire in advance.

Restaurants and shops around the park entrance often sell only simple drinks and snacks, so it's best to bring a packed lunch and water from San Miguel town or Manila. Downtown San Miguel has carinderias serving Filipino home cooking and fast-food chains. The region's pride is pastillas de leche, made from reduced carabao milk, and yema, made from egg yolk — both easy to buy at sweets shops along Maharlika Highway and popular gifts among expats.
The park is usually open around
8 AM–5 PM
, but hours can change by day and weather, so check the latest notices.
It's safer to have a guide assigned when you register for cave exploring. The paths branch in several directions, and it's easy to get lost going in alone.
Bring a headlamp, a change of clothes, shoes you don't mind getting wet, water and snacks, and a small trash bag.
The bat cave floor is muddy with droppings and the smell is strong. Wear a mask, and wash your hands after you come out.
Weekends and school breaks bring plenty of student groups. Go on a weekday morning for a quieter visit.
If traveling by public transport, getting a ride back is the biggest challenge. Get the phone number of your tricycle driver.
Pairing this with Barasoain Church makes it easier to follow the thread of the revolution from the Republic of Biak-na-Bato in 1897 to the Malolos Republic in 1899.
In
August 2026

the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) opened a new Protected Area Information Center (PAIC) in the park. When you register, ask the information center which caves are open and about the river level, and plan your route accordingly.

In the wet season, rain upstream can cause a flash flood that raises the river suddenly. If it rains or the water turns muddy, get out of the river immediately and move to higher ground, and avoid swimming in the afternoon.
Cave floors and riverside rocks are very slippery. Wear shoes with firm soles instead of sandals.
Don't touch or take stalactites or rock fragments inside the caves, and don't write on the walls.
The suspension bridge has a set limit on how many people can cross at once — follow the posted guidance.
The forest trails can have mosquitoes and leeches, so bring long pants and repellent.
Phone signal is weak in some sections, so stay with your group and follow your guide's instructions.
